timeline.event: Unauthorized access to the internal groupware occurred (as reported).
Flybit confirmed the leak and posted an apology (according to Seoul Economic Daily and Newsway).
Media reports made the incident public.

impact: Personal information of 40 customers was leaked (according to the company).
For individual customers, it included name, resident registration number and contact details. For corporate customers, it included company name and corporate registration number.
No crypto asset losses have been reported.
cause: It was reported that the outside attacker gained access by way of the groupware operator. The attack method, how the operator was breached and whether other client companies were affected have not been disclosed.
response: Flybit blocked the access path and temporarily blocked all access from overseas IP addresses. It asked the police to investigate and is working with the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and others. It notified affected customers separately by email and text.

overview: An online site where Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, Japan, sells charms and other souvenirs was accessed without authorization. About 14,500 member records were leaked (according to the shrine). The sales site, not the entire official website, was affected.
The shrine confirmed the unauthorized access on Oct 28 and closed the site that day. It posted a notice of the leak on its website on Nov 11. Korean media reported it on Nov 12.

The leaked information is names, emails, passwords stored as converted values (hash values) and account registration information. The shrine said card information was processed through a payment service provider and there are no traces of it being leaked.

timeline.event: Unauthorized access was confirmed, and the shrine closed the sales site.
The shrine posted a notice of the personal information leak on its website.
Korean media reported the incident.

impact: About 14,500 member records were leaked (according to the shrine). This may change depending on the investigation results.
Names, emails, password hash values, account registration times and account status were included.
No leak of card information, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth or purchase history has been confirmed.
cause: The intrusion method has not been disclosed. The shrine is investigating the cause with the company that manages the site.
response: The shrine notified members individually by email. It asked them to change their passwords on other services that use the same password and to watch out for messages impersonating the shrine. No date has been set for reopening the site.

overview: KB Capital's car rental asset management system was attacked from outside, and personal information was leaked. The system is an internal system used by employees and partner companies. The company said it is not related to its financial transaction systems.

While checking server load, the company found several suspicious lookup attempts coming from IP addresses in Korea (according to Dealsite). On Nov 10, it confirmed the leak, stopped the system and reported to the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS).

The leak affects 20 customers and 1,791 partner company staff and employees, 1,811 people in total (company's provisional count). The company explained that the number may fall slightly during final checks.

timeline.event: The company confirmed the leak, stopped the system and servers, and reported to the FSS (according to Dealsite and Sisa Journal).
The company posted a notice of the leak on its website. Media reported the notice date as either Nov 12 or Nov 13.
Media reports made the incident widely known.

impact: The leak affects 20 customers and 1,791 partner company staff and employees, 1,811 people in total (company's provisional count).
Customer information includes name, date of birth, mobile phone number, address and vehicle number.
Partner company staff and employee information includes account, name, phone number, department, company name and job title.
cause: The company explained that lookups came from IP addresses in Korea in a malicious outside attack. The intrusion path and method have not been disclosed.
response: The company blocked the access path and strengthened monitoring. It set up a lookup on its website where individuals can check whether their data was leaked, and apologized. It said it would fully compensate for any damage and is running a dedicated support center (according to Dealsite).

overview: An outside attacker gained unauthorized access to the systems of KakaoWork, a messenger for work. User information, email bodies and attachments, and encrypted messages were leaked (according to the company's notice). The victims are current and former Kakao Enterprise employees, outside people using company accounts and some email recipients.

On Nov 1, the provider of KakaoWork changed from DK Techin to Kakao. The incident was confirmed 8 days later, on Nov 9. In practice, DK Techin still runs the service as Kakao's contractor (according to News Tomato).

On Nov 12, the company reported to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and the Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) and issued a notice. The scale of the leak has not yet been finalized.

timeline.event: The provider of KakaoWork changed from DK Techin to Kakao.
Abnormal access and a leak were confirmed.
The company reported to KISA and the PIPC and notified users (according to Electronic Times).
Media reports made the incident widely known.

impact: The leaked items are name, nickname, department, mobile phone number, email address, email subject and body, attachment names and original files, and encrypted messages (according to the company's notice).

There was a report of 44 client companies and more than 5,000 users, but the company said these are not figures it has confirmed and announced, and that it is still investigating (according to Maeil Ilbo).
No password leak has been confirmed. Whether the encrypted messages were decrypted has not been confirmed either.
cause: Only the fact of abnormal access by an outside attacker is known. The intrusion path and method have not been disclosed and are under investigation.
response: The company blocked the access path and opened a page for checking whether one's data was leaked. It recommended that users change their passwords, told them to watch out for messages impersonating the company, and apologized.

The PIPC is looking into what happened and plans to examine the management and oversight of both DK Techin, which runs the service, and Kakao, which outsourced the work to it (according to News Tomato).

overview: An unauthorized outsider accessed "chak", the mobile local gift certificate platform run by Korea Minting and Security Printing Corporation (KOMSCO). Part of the personal information of 3,083 users was viewed (KOMSCO announcement, as of 6 a.m. on Nov 14). After confirming signs of access, KOMSCO briefly stopped the server service, then reopened it after emergency security measures.

The information viewed is some of the following: name, date of birth, mobile phone number, account number, connecting information (CI), email and encrypted card number. For 3,072 people, 2 or fewer items were exposed, and for 11 people, 3 to 4 items were exposed (according to KOMSCO).
Whether the information left the system and whether there were further leaks have not yet been confirmed. KOMSCO is investigating the intrusion path and method (according to Dailysecu).

timeline.event: Around 9:30 a.m., signs of abnormal access were confirmed. KOMSCO blocked the suspicious IP addresses and blocked all access from overseas IP addresses.
Around noon, KOMSCO shut down the targeted communication log management system for linked agencies, and it finished its emergency security measures around 10:38 p.m. (according to Edaily).
KOMSCO announced the incident and ran a temporary customer center from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m.

impact: Part of the personal information of 3,083 users was viewed (according to KOMSCO).
For 3,072 people, 2 or fewer items were exposed, and for 11 people, 3 to 4 items were exposed.
The items are name, date of birth, mobile phone number, account number, connecting information (CI), email and encrypted card number.
Chak is used by 84 local governments across Korea and has about 4.3 million users (according to Edaily).
No theft of gift certificate balances or fraudulent payments has been confirmed so far (according to Edaily).
cause: The attacker did not take over the servers directly. The attack targeted a weakness in the authentication of the APIs that servers use to talk to each other (according to Edaily).
The intrusion path and method, and whether there were further leaks, are under investigation. Whether the information was taken outside has not been confirmed either (according to Dailysecu).
response: KOMSCO reported to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and others and started 24-hour monitoring. It notified affected users individually and is running a dedicated customer center.
KOMSCO said it would analyze vulnerabilities with outside experts and improve access control, and apologized.
The president of KOMSCO apologized and promised to prevent a repeat. A dedicated call center explains how to claim damages and apply for personal information dispute mediation (according to Edaily).

overview: AmicusLex, a company that supplies an AI solution to "Startup for All", a startup support program of the Ministry of SMEs and Startups (MSS), was hacked. Information on 20,028 users of the company's legal document AI service was leaked. Of these, 818 are "Startup for All" participants (according to the MSS).
AmicusLex is one of 50 supplier companies selected by the MSS. The MSS explained that this system is run by the company itself and is separate from the program's official platform.
This is the second time information has leaked from "Startup for All". This incident was disclosed about 60 hours after it happened, which drew criticism that the disclosure was late (as reported).

timeline.event: The attack occurred at 5:38 a.m., and the company noticed it at 8:30 a.m. It reported to KISA at 3:45 p.m.
At 6:10 p.m., the company informed the Korea Institute of Startup & Entrepreneurship Development and the MSS of the incident.
Victims were notified individually at 3 p.m., and the MSS made an official announcement around 5 p.m.
It was reported that the MSS is considering canceling the company's selection and restricting its participation (according to Maeil Ilbo).

impact: Information on 20,028 users was leaked, and 818 of them are "Startup for All" participants (according to the MSS).
The leaked items are name, phone number and email.
cause: According to the company's leak report, attempts to extract information through SQL injection via the admin page were confirmed. The company deleted the vulnerable API code (as reported). Other details have not been disclosed.
response: The company blocked access from overseas IP addresses. The MSS is considering canceling the company's selection and restricting its participation for 1 year. The remaining 49 supplier companies are to be checked by Nov 20.
The MSS is guiding victims on remedies through its legal advisory group and has formed a dedicated security team led by the First Vice Minister.

overview: An outsider broke into the operations system of Fugaku, the supercomputer that Japan's RIKEN runs in Kobe. The intrusion took place between Nov 10 and Nov 13, 2026 (according to RIKEN). Early on Nov 14, RIKEN stopped Fugaku and cut off outside access.

According to RIKEN, names, email addresses and other information of up to 4,597 users of Fugaku and of RIKYU, an AI research supercomputer, were taken or may have been taken. Credentials that users had stored for outside access and some research data files were also affected. RIKEN said there is no specific evidence so far that research results have leaked outside.

Companies such as Toyota, Nippon Steel, Honda and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries also use Fugaku for research, which raised concerns about leaks of corporate technology (according to The Korea Economic Daily, citing Nikkei). It has not been confirmed whether these companies' data actually leaked. How the intruder got in and whether there was secondary damage are under investigation.

timeline.event: From this day to Nov 13, an outsider was inside Fugaku's operations network (according to RIKEN's investigation).
RIKEN detected suspicious communications and began an investigation with its outsourced maintenance contractor.

Unauthorized access was confirmed at 4:33 p.m. RIKEN reported to the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) at 8:59 p.m. and isolated the system used for the intrusion at 10:07 p.m.
At 4:30 a.m., Fugaku was stopped and outside access was cut off. Administrative keys were replaced at 8:20 p.m.
All running and queued jobs were stopped, and all users' login public keys were disabled. The same day, Toyota was told of the unauthorized access by RIKEN (according to The Korea Economic Daily).
RIKEN announced the incident and reported it to the Personal Information Protection Commission.

impact: Names, email addresses and IDs of up to 4,222 Fugaku users were taken or may have been taken (according to RIKEN).
Names and email addresses of up to 375 users of RIKYU, an AI research supercomputer, are also affected.
Some credentials for outside access (SSH private keys, access keys) stored in users' home directories are also affected.
Some research data files are also affected; their number has not been disclosed.
RIKEN said there is no specific evidence so far that research results have leaked outside.
It has not been confirmed whether research data of corporate users such as Toyota and Nippon Steel has leaked (according to The Korea Economic Daily and The Financial News).
Sumitomo Rubber Industries' computations were halted because Fugaku stopped (according to Nikkei xTECH).
cause: The intruder used a public web dashboard showing Fugaku's operating status as a foothold to enter the internal operations network (according to RIKEN). RIKEN said it will fix the software vulnerability that was exploited. The specific intrusion method is under investigation.

The intruder manipulated several internal servers and installed unauthorized programs on some of them. The intruder also tried to use some of the stolen credentials to connect to other systems. Whether this caused secondary damage is being investigated with outside organizations. The attacker's identity and purpose have not been revealed.
response: RIKEN stopped Fugaku and cut off outside access. It isolated the system used for the intrusion, replaced administrative keys and disabled all users' login public keys. It reported the incident to MEXT, HPCI-related organizations and the Personal Information Protection Commission, in that order (according to RIKEN).

RIKEN asked users to revoke SSH private keys and other credentials stored on Fugaku at the services they connect to, and to reissue them. It warned users about emails impersonating Fugaku or RIKEN. RIKEN said it never asks for passwords by email.

RIKEN said that before resuming operations it will fix the vulnerability, rebuild the compromised servers and review the network configuration. It also plans to introduce AI-based security measures. No date for resuming operations has been set. Japan's education minister said the government will quickly strengthen the security of research infrastructure (according to The Financial News).

overview: An outside attacker added malicious JavaScript to customer projects at Optimizely, a website experimentation and optimization platform. Optimizely said a vulnerability in its Web Experimentation product was exploited (according to the company's status page). Customer websites that load this script could pass the malicious code to their visitors' browsers.

Security firm Report URI reviewed 1,611 Optimizely script files and found malicious code in 188 of them. These files belong to 178 organizations. They include Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab and an HSBC insurance site (according to Report URI's analysis and BleepingComputer). Report URI said the real number may be higher.

This does not mean the internal systems of all 178 organizations were breached. The malicious code reached visitors through an outside script that each website loads. The number of affected visitors and the amount of card data taken have not been disclosed.

timeline.event: Around 4:21 a.m. UTC, Report URI first saw malicious code in an Optimizely script (according to Search Engine Journal).
From around 1:43 p.m. UTC, the injected script began targeting card details in payment forms (according to Search Engine Journal).
Optimizely identified the incident and blocked the vulnerable path. By around 11:11 p.m. UTC, all infected files were clean (according to Report URI's analysis).
At 1:02 a.m. UTC, Optimizely posted a security incident notice on its status page.

impact: Malicious code was found in 188 of 1,611 Optimizely script files (according to Report URI's analysis).
The infected files belong to 178 organizations, and the real number may be higher (according to Report URI's analysis).
By sector, they include 32 in banking and finance, 23 in technology and software, and 20 in retail (according to CBC News).
About USD 7,000 in crypto assets reached the attacker's wallets, but the amount actually stolen has not been confirmed (according to BleepingComputer).
The number of affected visitors and the amount of card data leaked have not been disclosed.
cause: Optimizely said a vulnerability in the account signup flow of its Web Experimentation product was exploited (according to the company's statement to BleepingComputer). The attacker used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. How a signup flaw allowed changes to existing customer projects has not been disclosed.

The malicious code was delivered through Optimizely's normal delivery network, so customer websites loaded it as usual. The code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses shown on the page with the attacker's addresses and to collect card details from payment forms. It could also collect browser cookies and screenshots and load attack tools aimed at iPhones and iPads (according to Report URI's analysis and BleepingComputer). The attacker has not been identified.
response: Optimizely blocked the vulnerable path and deployed a fix. It removed the injected code, ended active sessions, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts. It also used Cloudflare to block delivery of the malicious code (according to BleepingComputer).

Optimizely said it notified all affected customers and is continuing its investigation. Salesforce turned off Optimizely scripts in its preview and production environments. Salesforce said it will notify customers if it finds unauthorized data access (according to BleepingComputer).

overview: The work email system used by Korean government agencies was attacked from outside. Abnormal access was found on about 300 accounts (according to the Ministry of the Interior and Safety). The email system is run by the National Information Resources Service (NIRS).

The ministry believes the attacker came in through the poorly secured networks of some local governments. The investigation found that a flaw in single sign-on (SSO) was exploited along the way. SSO lets a user reach several work systems with one login.

The ministry reported the personal data leak to the Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) and notified the people affected. The types and amount of information leaked have not been disclosed. Whether email bodies or attachments were taken out has not been confirmed either (according to Dailysecu).

timeline.event: A partner agency notified the Ministry of the Interior and Safety that government work email and other systems had been hacked from outside.
The ministry announced the incident. It said it was running a joint inspection with the National Intelligence Service (NIS) and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA).

impact: Abnormal access was found on about 300 work email accounts (according to the Ministry of the Interior and Safety).
The ministry confirmed a personal data leak and reported it to the PIPC.
The types and amount of personal data leaked have not been disclosed.
Whether email bodies, attachments or internal documents were taken out has not been confirmed (according to Dailysecu).
cause: The attacker first got in through the poorly secured networks of some local governments. The investigation found the attacker then used a flaw in single sign-on (SSO) to reach the work email system run by NIRS (according to the Ministry of the Interior and Safety).

Which local government's network was used and the exact flaw have not been disclosed. The date of the first intrusion and the attacker's identity are also unknown. The exact cause is being investigated in the joint inspection.
response: The ministry cut unnecessary connections between local government servers and the work email system. It applied emergency security measures to the email system and stepped up security monitoring. It notified the people whose information was leaked.

The ministry is running a joint inspection with the NIS and KISA. They plan to check the first intrusion path, how the SSO flaw was exploited, further traces of hacking and any malware left behind. The ministry said it would find the cause and prepare measures to prevent a repeat, including improving SSO, by the end of the year.

overview: An unauthorized outsider illegally accessed the server of the integrated research management system of Kangwon National University's Industry-Academic Cooperation Foundation. User information stored on the server was taken outside (according to the university's notice). The foundation announced the leak on its website on Nov 15 and apologized.

The leaked information includes student and employee ID numbers, names, affiliation, position, employment and registration status, and date of birth. System management information such as user type codes, affiliation codes and last login times was also leaked (according to Kangwon Ilbo). The university said unique identifiers such as resident registration numbers, and sensitive information such as passwords, were not leaked.

As of Nov 15, 27 victims whose data included a birth date had been confirmed. The total number of people affected has not been disclosed (according to Kangwon Ilbo and Dailysecu). Some outlets reported the number of affected users as 27 (according to Kyunghyang Shinmun).

timeline.event: Around 6:22 a.m., an unauthorized outsider accessed the integrated research management system server and took user information (according to the university's notice).
The foundation announced the leak on its website and apologized.
Around 2:16 p.m., the foundation announced that it was suspending access to the integrated research management system for an emergency inspection (according to Dailysecu).

impact: As of Nov 15, 27 victims whose data included a birth date had been confirmed (according to Kangwon Ilbo).
The total number of people affected has not been disclosed.
The leaked items are student and employee ID numbers, names, affiliation, position, employment and registration status, date of birth, and system management information.
The university said resident registration numbers and passwords were not leaked.
With access to the system suspended, research fund applications, spending and settlements may be disrupted (according to Dailysecu).
cause: Only the fact that an unauthorized outsider illegally accessed the system server has been disclosed. The intrusion path and method have not been revealed.

Around the same time on the same day, 6:22 a.m., several other universities, including Hankyong National University, Daegu Haany University and Korea Maritime and Ocean University, announced breaches of their research administration systems. That chain of incidents has its own story. Whether it is the same attack as Kangwon's has not been confirmed (according to Dailysecu and Boannews).
response: The foundation blocked the outside access path and checked for vulnerabilities. It is re-checking access rights and strengthening reviews of access logs. It said it would also prepare measures to prevent a recurrence, including training for staff who handle personal information (according to Kyunghyang Shinmun and Kangwon Ilbo).

It reported the incident to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), the Ministry of Education and other relevant agencies. It said it would ask investigative authorities to investigate if necessary (according to Kyunghyang Shinmun).

The head of the foundation apologized and said the foundation would review its personal information protection system from the ground up. The foundation asked users not to respond to calls, text messages or emails impersonating it, and to change their passwords on other sites where they use the same password.

overview: MetaM, the contractor that runs the customer center system for coffee franchise Mega MGC Coffee, was attacked from outside. The attacker went through MetaM's servers into the management functions of the customer center system. In the process, the mobile phone numbers of 30 customers who had called the customer center were leaked (according to the company).

The company said customer names, consultation content, call recordings and payment information were not leaked. However, numbers kept in customer center call records, and mobile numbers and email addresses entered in franchise inquiries on its website, may also have been leaked. The company is still investigating this (according to Newstomato and Segye Ilbo).
Mega MGC Coffee learned of the incident from the contractor on Nov 15, three days after the intrusion. The company announced it on its website on Nov 17 and apologized.

timeline.event: From 2:18 a.m. to 3:50 a.m., an outside attacker went through MetaM's servers into the management functions of the customer center system (according to the company). MetaM blocked the attack path the same day (according to Alphabiz).
MetaM informed Mega MGC Coffee of the incident.
Bunjang, which also used the same contractor for customer support, announced that customer phone numbers had been leaked (according to Alphabiz).
Mega MGC Coffee announced the incident on its website and apologized.

impact: The mobile phone numbers of 30 customers were leaked (according to the company).
All of the leaked numbers belong to customers who called the customer center.
The company said names, consultation content, call recordings and payment information were not leaked.
Whether numbers in call records, and mobile numbers and email addresses left in franchise inquiries, were leaked is under investigation.
cause: An outside attacker reportedly went through the servers of the contractor MetaM into the management functions of the customer center system (according to Segye Ilbo and Alphabiz). The attacker and the intrusion method have not been disclosed.
MetaM also handles customer support for other companies. Bunjang said customer phone numbers were also leaked in the same server intrusion (according to Alphabiz).
response: The attack path was blocked, server and database passwords were changed, and access was restricted. Access control on the management functions of the customer center phone system was also strengthened. Mega MGC Coffee said it checked the PCs connected to its own systems and found no signs of intrusion (according to Newstomato and Alphabiz).

The incident was reported to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and the Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) (according to Segye Ilbo and Newstomato). The company said it would notify customers whose data was confirmed or possibly leaked individually, by text message and other means, by Nov 18. It is also running a 24-hour damage consultation line (according to Alphabiz).

The company apologized to customers and said it would greatly strengthen security checks and oversight of its contractors. It asked customers to watch out for calls and text messages impersonating the company or its customer center.

overview: An outside service that the City of Osaka's "Administrative Online System" used to send email was accessed without authorization. The system is provided by TKC, and its email was sent through an email delivery service run by Arara (according to the City of Osaka). The city said no unauthorized access to its own system or to TKC's data center has been confirmed.

In its final report on Nov 13, the city said 1,078,713 user email addresses were leaked. The addresses are those that received email from the system between Jul 1 and Oct 31, 2026. It was confirmed that email bodies, My Number information and application information were not leaked (according to the City of Osaka).

Arara said about 77 million email addresses from nearly 400 customers were taken in the breach. The attacker used Arara's email delivery service to send millions of emails impersonating card companies and financial institutions (according to Boannews). The attacker's identity has not been revealed.

timeline.event: Arara confirmed unauthorized access to part of the servers of its email delivery service "Arara Message" (according to ScanNetSecurity).
Around 5:40 p.m., emergency maintenance began to stop the damage from spreading. From then on, the city's system could not send email (according to the City of Osaka).
TKC reported to the city that user information may have been leaked.
In its first report, the city said email addresses, names and other information may have been leaked.
In its second report, the city said the only information that may have leaked was email addresses. It said email bodies, My Number information and application information were not leaked.
In its final report, the city said 1,078,713 email addresses were leaked.

impact: 1,078,713 email addresses of users of the city's Administrative Online System were leaked (according to the City of Osaka).
The affected people are those who received email from the system between Jul 1 and Oct 31, 2026.
The city explained that the count is large because a notice was emailed to all registered users on Sep 16.
It was confirmed that email bodies, My Number information and application information were not leaked (according to the City of Osaka).
Because email sending stopped, users could not register, change their email address or reset their password in the system (according to the city's second report).
The city's premium gift voucher program, which used the same service, also had email addresses leaked: about 34,000 of users and about 15,000 of participating stores (according to Kyodo News).
The number of email addresses taken from the whole Arara service rose to 81,329,467 (according to ScanNetSecurity).
cause: The intrusion happened not at the city or TKC but at Arara, the outside service that sent the email. Arara explained that a third party exploited a web server vulnerability and problems in part of its system environment (according to ScanNetSecurity). The specific vulnerability and the attacker's identity have not been disclosed.
response: The city said it will keep requiring TKC to report the cause, the scope of the damage and measures to prevent a recurrence in detail. It will also review how the outside service handles personal information, its safety management measures and how the city works with the provider. How to notify the affected users directly is under consideration (according to the City of Osaka).

The city urged people to be careful of suspicious emails impersonating the city or the system. It told them not to open links or attachments in such emails and not to enter IDs, passwords or card information. The city said it will not tell people individually whether their address is affected.

overview: Around Nov 14, the research administration systems of several universities' industry-academic cooperation foundations were attacked one after another. Hallym University, Sookmyung Women's University, Hankyong National University, Daegu Haany University and Korea Maritime and Ocean University, Pusan National University and Dong-eui University announced that users' personal data had been leaked. Hankuk University of Foreign Studies found signs of a data leak and shut its system down, and Hannam University announced a security breach and suspended the service. Incheon National University blocked access to its system as a precaution (according to Dailysecu). Kangwon National University also announced that user information had been leaked from its integrated research management system on the same day.

The affected systems are research administration systems used for research fund management, accounting, budgeting and settlement. Hallym, Hannam, Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, Daegu Haany and Korea Maritime and Ocean University named the affected system as rERP. rERP is a system shared by many universities' industry-academic cooperation foundations (according to Boannews). Kangwon, Daegu Haany, Hankyong and Korea Maritime and Ocean University all gave the same first breach time, 6:22 a.m. on Nov 14 (according to Dailysecu).

The leaked items differ by university but mainly include student and employee ID numbers, names, affiliation, position, sign-up date and date of birth. Hallym, Sookmyung, Daegu Haany and Korea Maritime and Ocean University said resident registration numbers and passwords were not leaked. Whether the attacks were the work of the same attacker, or came through a common supplier or maintenance environment, has not been confirmed.

timeline.event: Around 4 a.m., an unauthorized outsider accessed the server of the company that manages Hallym University's integrated research administration system and took information (according to the university's notice and Kangwon Domin Ilbo).

Kangwon, Daegu Haany, Hankyong and Korea Maritime and Ocean University and Pusan National University each said the breach of their system happened around 6:22 a.m. (according to Dailysecu and Busan Ilbo).

Around 10:30 a.m., the system maker Webcash detected the attack and notified Daegu Haany University. Hankuk University of Foreign Studies suspended its research fund management system from 1 p.m. (according to Dailysecu).

Around 10 p.m., Hankyong National University learned of the incident through its maintenance company. Sookmyung Women's University was notified of the breach by the system maker around 10:12 p.m. (according to Dailysecu).
A hacker using the name 'KimJEN' posted on a hacking forum claiming to have obtained data from Korean universities (according to Dailysecu).
Around 11:14 a.m., Hallym University was notified of the incident after the managing company confirmed it. Daegu Haany University and Kangwon National University announced the leak on their websites.
Incheon National University fully blocked access to its research administration ERP, citing signs that a maintenance company's server had been hacked (according to Dailysecu).
Hallym, Sookmyung, Hankyong, Hannam and Korea Maritime and Ocean University announced the breach or the leak on their websites (according to Dailysecu).
Boannews reported an analysis of the files the attacker posted. The names of 28 universities were found in the files, and the folders for 17 of them contained information taken from rERP.
Dong-eui University posted an apology on its website and let affected people check whether their data was leaked (according to Dailysecu).
The scale of the leaks at Pusan National, Dong-eui and Korea Maritime and Ocean University was reported together (according to Busan Ilbo and Nocut News).

impact: Hallym University said 947 records were leaked, 83 of which included a date of birth (according to Kangwon Domin Ilbo and Dailysecu).
Sookmyung Women's University also announced that user data was leaked (according to Dailysecu).
Hankyong National University said 772 records of research fund management system users were leaked (according to Dailysecu).
Daegu Haany University said 1,281 records were leaked, 30 of which included a date of birth (according to Dailysecu).
Kangwon National University confirmed 27 victims whose data included a date of birth and did not disclose the total scale of the leak.
Korea Maritime and Ocean University said 1,359 records were leaked, 1,253 of which included a date of birth (according to Jaekyung Ilbo).
Pusan National University said 500 records were leaked, holding employee or student ID numbers, names, department names and sign-up dates (according to Busan Ilbo).

Dong-eui University said the information of 530 people was leaked, including employee ID numbers, names, departments, positions, titles, employment status and dates of birth (according to Dailysecu and Busan Ilbo).
Hannam University and Hankuk University of Foreign Studies did not disclose the leaked items or the scale of the damage.

The counts are per user record, so the same person may appear more than once and the actual number of people affected may differ (according to the Hallym and Korea Maritime and Ocean University notices).
With the systems shut down, research administration work such as research fund applications, spending and settlements may be disrupted (according to Dailysecu).
cause: The universities have disclosed only that an unauthorized outsider accessed their servers. Hallym University said the server of the company that manages the system was breached. Hankyong National University said the attacker got into the server through a web vulnerability, altered some files and created unauthorized files (according to Dailysecu).

Daegu Haany University learned of the incident when the system maker, Webcash, detected it and notified the university. Incheon National University blocked access citing signs that a maintenance company's server had been hacked. Whether a supplier's central server was taken over or a maintenance account was stolen has not been confirmed (according to Dailysecu and Boannews).

The hacker 'KimJEN' posted compressed files on a hacking forum, claiming to have stolen data from Korean universities. The files contain the names of 28 universities, including all of the universities that have reported incidents in this case (according to Boannews). Boannews reported that the attacker is believed to have collected the information by repeatedly calling query functions with authentication sessions and accounts obtained in advance. However, whether the data is genuine, and whether these incidents were KimJEN's work, has not been confirmed.
response: Hallym University shut down its web application server and deleted unauthorized files and abnormal schedulers. It removed the vulnerable web application and changed its database encryption and decryption keys. Hankuk University of Foreign Studies also deleted files related to the breach and abnormal schedulers, and urgently blocked the affected servers (according to Dailysecu).

Sookmyung Women's University and Daegu Haany University physically disconnected the affected servers from the network and stopped the service. Hankyong National University deleted abnormal files, temporarily stopped running a secondary server and strengthened its authentication process. Korea Maritime and Ocean University restricted access to the system and formed an emergency response team (according to Dailysecu).

Pusan National University blocked the attacker's IP address, made the system reachable only from campus and reset the passwords of all accounts. Dong-eui University also restricted access to the system and formed an emergency response team (according to Nocut News).

Hallym, Hankyong and Daegu Haany said they reported the incident to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and the Ministry of Education. Daegu Haany, Korea Maritime and Ocean University and others asked users not to respond to calls, text messages or emails impersonating the university or its foundation. They also asked users to change their passwords on other sites where they use the same password.

overview: An outside vendor that provides services to JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard was hacked. Some customers' names, email addresses and other marketing data stored with the vendor were exposed (according to The Wall Street Journal and the companies). The three companies did not name the vendor.

Visa said an outside vendor that provides services in the Asia-Pacific region was attacked and that its own systems were not affected. Mastercard said limited non-payment information of some cardholders was exposed and that its payment network is operating normally (according to Newspim and Yonhap).

The ransomware group 'n0n' claimed responsibility. However, whether it was really behind the attack, and whether the data it published is genuine, has not been confirmed (according to The Financial News and CWN).

timeline.event: JPMorgan Chase had a transaction processing outage. JPMorgan said the outage was caused by a software error and is unrelated to this hack (according to CWN).
n0n claimed it took cardholder-related records on this day (according to The Financial News).
The Wall Street Journal reported the vendor hack (US local time). The three companies confirmed that some customer information was exposed (according to The Financial News and Newspim).

impact: The companies said the exposed information is marketing data such as customers' names and email addresses.
Visa and Mastercard said payment data such as card numbers was not leaked.
Data reviewed by Reuters contained about 16,000 email addresses that appear to belong to JPMorgan customers (according to The Financial News and CWN).
The same data also held 124 email addresses that appear to belong to JPMorgan employees. Reuters could not verify whether the data is genuine (according to CWN).
The number of customers affected and the exact scope of the leak have not been disclosed.
JPMorgan said the incident did not interrupt its services.
cause: An attacker got into the systems of an outside vendor that serves the three companies and accessed marketing data stored there (according to JPMorgan and Yonhap). How the attacker got into the vendor has not been disclosed.

The ransomware group n0n claimed the attack. Security firm Recorded Future described n0n as an extortion group that shares its profits with sellers of initial access (according to Global Economic and Newspim). Whether n0n was really behind the attack has not been confirmed.
response: JPMorgan is reportedly notifying affected customers individually and considering offering free credit monitoring (according to CWN). Mastercard said it stopped further leakage and is working with its service providers to support affected cardholders (according to Global Economic and Yonhap).

overview: A training management site used to train savings bank staff was hacked from outside. The site is run by KG Eduone, a company that specialises in training. Some staff names, the savings banks they work for and their job titles were leaked (according to Seoul Economic Daily).

The Korea Federation of Savings Banks announced this on its website on Nov 18. The incident happened on an outside training platform, not on the savings banks' internal networks (according to Newsis and Aju Business Daily).

The federation warned that the leaked data could be used by fraudsters posing as savings bank staff to approach customers. It asked people not to trust a caller just because they give a real employee's name and bank (according to Newsis).

timeline.event: The Korea Federation of Savings Banks posted a notice on its website about the hack of the training management site and the leak of staff information (according to Aju Business Daily).
Seoul Economic Daily and other outlets reported the incident. When the hack happened has not been disclosed.

impact: The leaked information is staff names, the savings banks they work for and their job titles (according to Seoul Economic Daily and Newsis).
The number of people affected, the number of savings banks affected and the time of the hack have not been disclosed.
The federation is concerned about follow-on fraud such as voice phishing and smishing by people posing as staff.
cause: An outside training management site used to train savings bank staff was hacked. The method and time of the intrusion have not been disclosed. The incident reportedly did not happen on the savings banks' own networks (according to Newsis).
response: The Korea Federation of Savings Banks asked customers to be careful with calls and text messages from people posing as staff. It warned in particular about contacts claiming to check for data leaks, set up financial safety measures, offer loan consultations or pay compensation. It asked people not to tap links from unknown sources or install remote-control apps (according to Newsis and Global Economy Newspaper).

The federation said savings banks never ask for account passwords, security card numbers, one-time passwords (OTP) or verification codes by phone or text message. It advised checking whether a person really works at a savings bank through the bank's official website or main phone number when in doubt.

overview: An outside attacker gained unauthorized access to the business systems of Kurly, an online grocery company. On Nov 20, 2026, Kurly said the personal data of 10,699 participants in its curator program was leaked. The member numbers of 2 general customers were also leaked (according to Kurly).

Curators are affiliate marketers who introduce Kurly products on their social media channels and earn money by sharing purchase links (according to ZDNet Korea). Besides names and contact details, the leaked data includes bank account numbers and resident registration numbers or business registration numbers of some curators.

Kurly said it would give curators reward points worth 50,000 to 150,000 won each. CEO Kim Seul-ah issued an apology. The investigation into the cause and checks on whether the data has spread outside are ongoing.

timeline.event: An outside attacker got into Kurly's systems by abnormal means and stole credentials. The attacker used them to access business systems without authorization (according to Kurly).
Kurly said it took emergency blocking measures right after it became aware of the incident. The exact time of detection has not been disclosed.
Kurly reported the breach to the relevant authorities.
Kurly announced the leak and its compensation plan, and CEO Kim Seul-ah issued an apology.

impact: The names, IDs, phone numbers, email addresses and social media channel details of 10,699 curators were leaked (according to Kurly).
For some curators, bank account numbers and resident registration numbers or business registration numbers were also leaked. How many has not been disclosed.
For 2 general customers, only member numbers were leaked (according to Kurly).
Kurly said the names, contact details, addresses, passwords and payment details of the 2 general customers were not leaked.
Kurly explained that it does not collect general customers' resident registration numbers or bank account numbers (according to ZDNet Korea).
cause: Kurly explained that an outside attacker got into its systems by abnormal means and stole credentials. The attacker used them to access business systems without authorization. Further investigation confirmed the personal data leak, and access to the related documents was blocked (according to Electronic Times).

How the credentials were stolen and the name of the system that was breached have not been disclosed. How long the attacker had access has not been revealed either. The attacker's identity and the exact cause are still under investigation.
response: Kurly said it would give each curator reward points worth at least 50,000 won and up to 150,000 won, depending on the scope of the leak. The points can be used in the Kurly app for one year without conditions (according to Segye Ilbo). Kurly said it would pay the full amount of any actual damage caused by the leak. It will give separate guidance on legal remedies.

Kurly opened an information page for curators and a dedicated customer center. It plans to notify the 2 general customers individually. In her apology, CEO Kim Seul-ah said she was sorry the company had failed to protect customers' information.

Kurly said it had set up an emergency communication structure led by the CEO and the heads of the departments involved. It said it would check whether the leaked data has spread outside and work with the authorities to delete or block it. It also plans to investigate the cause and review its overall security.

overview: At Paichai University in Daejeon, the learning management system (LMS) and the academic system linked to it were hacked from outside. Some personal information of students and staff stored in the two systems was taken (according to the university's notice and Chungnam Ilbo). The university posted a notice about the leak and an apology on its website on Nov 18.

From the LMS, student and staff ID numbers, names, email addresses and affiliations were leaked. From the academic system, user IDs, encrypted passwords and dates of birth were leaked (according to Chungnam Ilbo and Dailysecu). The university said resident registration numbers, passport numbers, driver's license numbers and foreign resident registration numbers were not leaked.

The exact number of people and records affected has not yet been confirmed (according to Dailysecu). Several universities have recently suffered similar hacks, but no link to the Paichai incident has been confirmed.

timeline.event: Between 9 a.m. and 11:12 p.m., personal information in the LMS and the academic system was leaked in an outside hack (according to Chungnam Ilbo and Dailysecu).
From 9 a.m., two-factor authentication became mandatory for portal logins (according to ZDNet Korea).
From 3 p.m., passwords of user accounts began to be reset. The same day, the university posted a notice about the leak and an apology on its website (according to ZDNet Korea and Dailysecu).
Chungnam Ilbo, ZDNet Korea, Dailysecu and others reported the incident.

impact: The number of people and records affected has not been disclosed.
Student and staff ID numbers, names, email addresses and affiliations were leaked from the LMS (according to Chungnam Ilbo).
User IDs, encrypted passwords and dates of birth were leaked from the academic system (according to Chungnam Ilbo).
The university said resident registration numbers, passport numbers, driver's license numbers and foreign resident registration numbers were not leaked.
Whether the encrypted passwords can be decrypted, and whether the attacker actually logged into any accounts, has not been confirmed (according to Dailysecu).
cause: Only the fact that personal information was leaked in an outside hack has been disclosed. When the university first detected the attack, the intrusion path and how the data was taken have not been revealed. It is also not confirmed which system the attacker entered first, or whether the link between the two systems was used in the attack (according to Dailysecu).
response: The university isolated the two affected systems from the external network. It made two-factor authentication mandatory for portal logins and reset the passwords of all user accounts. To avoid confusion over class attendance, teaching staff and enrolled undergraduates were asked to change their passwords themselves (according to Chungnam Ilbo and ZDNet Korea).

The university reported the incident to the Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA). It informed its privacy officer and the relevant departments and activated its internal emergency response system. It is notifying data subjects individually and plans to provide a lookup function for checking which items were leaked (according to Dailysecu and ZDNet Korea).

A university official said the university takes the matter seriously and will strengthen its personal information protection system to prevent a recurrence. It also plans security checks of websites run by its departments and new security policies (according to Chungnam Ilbo).

overview: At Yeungnam University in the Daegu-Gyeongbuk region, the library e-book website and the job website were hacked from outside. Personal information of students and staff held on the two sites was taken (according to the university's notice and Dailysecu). The university posted a notice about the leak and an apology on its website on Nov 17.

The leaked items differ slightly between reports. Student ID numbers, names and affiliations were reported by all, and some reports say mobile phone numbers and email addresses were also included (according to Dailysecu and Seoul Shinmun). The Financial News reported that passwords were also leaked from the e-book website.

The university found that unique identifiers such as resident registration numbers were not leaked (according to Seoul Shinmun and The Financial News). The exact number of people affected is still under investigation. Kyungil University and Daegu Haany University were also hacked around the same time, but no link to the Yeungnam incident has been confirmed.

timeline.event: Between 10 a.m. and noon, the library e-book website and the job website were hacked (according to Dailysecu and The Financial News).
At 5:32 p.m., the university posted a notice about the leak and an apology on its website (according to Dailysecu).
Yonhap, Seoul Shinmun, The Financial News and others reported the incident along with a series of hacks at universities in the Daegu-Gyeongbuk region.

impact: The number of people and records affected has not been disclosed. The university is removing duplicates to count the exact scale (according to The Financial News).
Student ID numbers, names and affiliations were leaked (according to Dailysecu, Seoul Shinmun and The Financial News).
Some reports say mobile phone numbers and email addresses were also leaked (according to Seoul Shinmun).
Passwords were also leaked from the e-book website (according to The Financial News).
Unique identifiers such as resident registration numbers were found not to have been leaked (according to Seoul Shinmun).
cause: Only the fact that the two websites were compromised by an outside hack has been disclosed. The initial intrusion path and the access the attacker gained have not been revealed. It is also not confirmed whether both sites were breached through the same vulnerability, or whether one system was used to reach the other (according to Dailysecu).

Research administration systems at many university industry-academic cooperation foundations have recently been attacked one after another. Dailysecu reported that no sign has been found linking this incident to that series or to a hacker who claimed to have obtained data from Korean universities.
response: After confirming the incident, the university isolated and blocked the affected websites. It plans to force portal password changes and add two-factor authentication to logins (according to Dailysecu and Seoul Shinmun).

The university apologized and said it would review its personal information protection system from the ground up to prevent a recurrence. It asked members to change their passwords on other sites where they use the same password, and to report any suspected misuse right away (according to The Financial News).

overview: Internal staff systems of the European Union's European Commission were hit by a cyberattack. Sysper, the HR system that handles payslips, working hours and leave, and MyPMO, the medical reimbursement system, went down. The disruption lasted more than 10 days (according to Politico).

CERT-EU, the cybersecurity team for EU institutions, found that a tool called ARTEX was used in the attack. ARTEX is an AI-based penetration testing tool that anyone can get. It finds security weaknesses in systems automatically (according to Politico).
The Commission acknowledged the attack. However, it did not say who was behind it. Whether staff personal data was taken has not yet been confirmed.

timeline.event: The Commission first detected the attack (according to a Commission spokesperson, as reported by heise).
The Commission confirmed the attack (according to a Commission spokesperson, as reported by heise).
The Commission's translation services were also disrupted (according to Cyber Security News).
The Sysper HR system, which had been restored, briefly went down again (according to Cyber Security News).
Politico reported the attack and the use of ARTEX. Several other outlets followed.
Korean outlets such as Boannews reported the incident.

impact: Some staff could not enter working hours or request leave for more than 10 days (according to Politico).
Sysper, the HR system that handles payslips, went down.
MyPMO, the medical reimbursement system, went down.
Salaries were largely paid as usual (according to Cyber Security News).
Most systems have been restored.
Whether staff personal data was leaked has not been confirmed. A Commission spokesperson said there was no evidence of a breach affecting staff as a whole (according to Neowin).
cause: CERT-EU found that the AI penetration testing tool ARTEX was used in the attack. However, it is not known whether the tool was used to break in or only to look for weaknesses (according to Cyber Security News).

ARTEX has been taken down from GitHub, but copies are reported to still be circulating (according to Neowin). The attacker's identity and motive have not been disclosed. The exact intrusion path is still under investigation.
response: The Commission confirmed the attack. Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said individual systems were targeted. He said the affected parties had been informed (according to Cyber Security News).
Regnier did not name the attacker. He said he had no knowledge of any ransom demand (according to Neowin). The Commission and CERT-EU are still investigating the extent of the damage.

overview: The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating signs that an outsider broke into its National Crime Information Center (NCIC). Two people briefed on the investigation said so. They suspect hackers were behind it (according to CNN).

The NCIC is a network shared by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies. Police officers use it every day to check for fugitives and warrants. It holds millions of criminal records (according to IBTimes).

In the same week, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) was also hit by a cyberattack. A system that pays farmers was targeted (according to NBC). Whether the two incidents are linked has not been confirmed.

timeline.event: The hacking group ShinyHunters went after staff personal data through an FBI jobs website. The FBI said it was investigating (according to ABC).
The USDA told employees that one of its systems had been attacked (according to NBC).
CNN first reported the FBI's investigation into the NCIC intrusion. NBC followed, also reporting the USDA attack.
President Trump said he had only recently learned of the FBI breach (according to AFP). Korean outlets such as Yonhap reported the incident.

impact: Signs of an outside intrusion were found in the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) (according to CNN).
What information was accessed has not been confirmed.
The possibility that records were altered was raised. However, no actual alteration has been confirmed (according to Yonhap).
The USDA's system for paying farmers was attacked (according to NBC).
The USDA said no other systems had been attacked (according to NBC).
The USDA's position is that no personal data or other data was leaked (according to Yonhap).
cause: Who broke in has not been disclosed. No group has claimed responsibility yet (according to NBC). The intrusion path has not been made public either.

In the same week, the US saw a series of major outages in travel, communications and online shopping. Officials repeatedly said those outages were not linked to criminal activity. The FBI and USDA incidents, by contrast, were reported to appear malicious (according to AFP).
response: The FBI is investigating the signs of intrusion. As of the night the reports came out, the FBI had not commented (according to NBC).

The USDA acknowledged that a cybersecurity incident had occurred (according to Yonhap). The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) referred questions to the USDA (according to NBC).
President Trump said the FBI breach was not good. He urged people to relax (according to AFP).

overview: An outsider gained unauthorised access to the systems of LK Insurance Brokerage, the broker that handled group policies for Yebyeol Insurance (formerly MG Insurance). Personal data of people insured under a past group accident policy leaked as a result (according to Yebyeol Insurance).

Those affected are 66 people insured under a group accident policy taken out in July 2021 that ended in July 2022. The leaked data includes names, resident registration numbers, dates of birth, gender, mobile numbers, login IDs and employer names. The exact items differ from person to person (according to Aju Business Daily and Shinailbo).
All reports describe the contractor's systems. None says that Yebyeol Insurance's own systems were breached.

timeline.event: Unauthorised access to LK Insurance Brokerage's systems began (according to Aju Business Daily).
The access continued until this day, the third day.
Yebyeol Insurance disclosed the leak in a notice on its website and to the press.

impact: Personal data of 66 people insured under a past group accident policy leaked (according to Yebyeol Insurance).
The leaked items include resident registration numbers and mobile numbers.
No damage to Yebyeol Insurance's own systems has been reported.
cause: The outsider reportedly broke into a group insurance claims service run by the contractor (according to Aju Business Daily). The attacker and the exact method have not been disclosed.
response: LK Insurance Brokerage closed the access path used in the intrusion and fixed the security flaw. It also blocked the attacking IP addresses and overseas access, Yebyeol Insurance said (according to Aju Business Daily).

Yebyeol Insurance reported the incident to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and the Personal Information Protection Commission. It said it notified the affected customers individually. It also said it would tighten oversight of the contractor (according to Edaily).

overview: The official website of HD Hyundai Robotics, an industrial robot maker, was accessed unlawfully from outside. The personal data of website members was leaked as a result. The company said the leak happened on Nov 19, 2026, and was confirmed the next day (according to EBN).

The leaked data covers up to 10 items, including names, user IDs, mobile phone numbers and email addresses. It also includes affiliation details such as company names, department names and job titles (according to Dailysecu). Passwords were encrypted.
The number of affected people and the intrusion route have not been disclosed. The company said it is working out exactly how the incident happened and how far the damage goes.

timeline.event: Website member data was leaked through unlawful outside access (according to the company). iNews24 reported that the company spotted signs of the unlawful access on this day.
The company confirmed that members' personal data had been leaked (according to EBN).
The company posted a notice of the leak and an apology on its website, and media reports followed.

impact: The leaked items are member type, name, user ID, encrypted password, company name, company landline number, department name, job title, mobile phone number and email address (according to Dailysecu).
The items actually leaked may differ from member to member.
The number of affected people has not been disclosed.
A company official said part of the leaked data had been masked (according to iNews24).
A company official said no secondary damage, such as impersonation fraud, had been reported so far (according to iNews24).
cause: The company said part of its members' data was leaked through unlawful outside access to its website. The initial intrusion route and the vulnerability used have not been disclosed.
There is no confirmation that the company's internal network, robot control systems or production facilities were breached (according to Dailysecu). The exact cause is under investigation.
response: Right after detecting the abnormal access, the company blocked the IP addresses used in the attack and isolated the related server. It also tightened outside access controls and security monitoring (according to iNews24).

The company posted a notice of the leak on its website and is guiding members on how to check whether they are affected and which items were leaked (according to Pinpoint News). It advised members to change their passwords and to be wary of impersonation attempts.

The company said it would cooperate fully with the authorities' investigation. It said it would strengthen its data protection through further security checks. Whether and when it reported the incident to the authorities was not reported.

overview: Signs of an outside intrusion were found in the 'Voice of Customer' (VOC) system on Samsung Securities' website. The VOC system is where customers file complaints and feedback. Samsung Securities disclosed this on Nov 23, 2026.

Some of the files customers attached when filing complaints were taken out. As a result, the personal data of 8,241 customers was leaked (according to the company). The leaked data covers up to 13 items, including names, addresses, contact numbers, bank account numbers and driver's license numbers.

The company said traces of the leak were found only in data submitted through the VOC system. It said customers who never used the VOC system are not affected. The intrusion route and cause are under investigation.

timeline.event: Samsung Securities found signs of an outside intrusion in the 'Voice of Customer' system on its website. The company blocked the IP addresses used in the intrusion and suspended the service (according to Korea Credit News).
Samsung Securities announced that the personal data of 8,241 customers had been leaked. CEO Park Jong-moon posted an apology on the website (according to Insight Korea).

impact: The personal data of 8,241 customers was leaked (according to the company).
The leaked data covers up to 13 items, including names, addresses, contact numbers, bank account numbers and driver's license numbers.
The items actually leaked differ from person to person, depending on the files each customer uploaded.
The company said customers who never used the VOC system are not affected by the leak.
cause: The company said an unauthorized outsider accessed the VOC system. Some attached files uploaded by customers, such as photos, were taken out (according to Youth Daily).
When the intrusion began and what method was used have not been disclosed. The exact cause and how the data was leaked are under investigation.
response: Right after detecting the incident, Samsung Securities blocked the IP addresses used in the intrusion and suspended the related service. It reported the incident to the Financial Supervisory Service and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), among others. The date of the reports was not disclosed (according to Insight Korea).

The company decided to notify affected customers individually of what was leaked. It was also reported that customers can check on the website whether they are affected (according to Korea Credit News). A dedicated call center began taking damage reports.

The company said it is running a company-wide security review to check whether other systems saw similar intrusion attempts. It said it would compensate customers under the relevant laws and its internal rules if actual damage is confirmed (according to Segye Ilbo).

overview: An outsider illegally broke into Hana Savings Bank's mobile web system for customer re-verification. The system is used to check and update existing customers' information again. The bank said it found the intrusion on Nov 16 (according to the bank's notice, News1 and Jaekyung Ilbo).

The personal data of 552 customers was leaked. Nineteen items were leaked, including name, resident registration number, phone number and address. The items leaked may differ from customer to customer (according to the bank's notice).
The bank is investigating whether more customers' data was leaked. The number of people affected may therefore rise (according to News1).

timeline.event: The bank found that an outsider had broken into its mobile web customer re-verification system (according to the bank's notice).
The bank posted an apology on its website. It notified the affected customers individually by mobile phone or post (according to Jaekyung Ilbo and Hankyung).
The bank announced the leak in a notice on its website, and the media reported the incident.

impact: The personal data of 552 customers was leaked (according to the bank's notice).
Nineteen items were leaked, including name, English name, date of birth, resident registration number, phone number, home address, employer name, work address and email (according to Dailysecu).
The range of items leaked may differ from customer to customer.
Whether more data was leaked is still under investigation.
Concerns were raised that the data could be misused for identity theft, voice phishing, or pharming that lures people to fake websites (according to Hankyung).
Since late September, breaches have been confirmed at five savings banks: Yegaram, Welcome, DB, OK and now Hana. In total, 46,514 records were leaked (according to Hankyung).
cause: An outsider illegally broke into the mobile web customer re-verification system. The vulnerability used, the intrusion route and the time of the first intrusion have not been disclosed. It has also not been disclosed whether internal systems were affected (according to Dailysecu).
response: The bank blocked access from the outside IP addresses. It said it has taken further security measures and strengthened 24-hour monitoring. It is also preparing a relief procedure for victims (according to the bank's notice and Jaekyung Ilbo).

The bank asked customers to watch out for phishing text messages and impersonation. It also pointed them to identity-theft prevention services: the exposed-data accident prevention system, the non-face-to-face account opening block and the loan transaction block (according to Dailysecu).

overview: It became known that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) were hit by a hack. The New York Times reported this on Nov 24, 2026 (local time), citing government officials and people familiar with the matter. The Associated Press (AP) also reported, citing a source, that an unclassified CIA system had been attacked.

The system affected is reportedly an open-source intelligence (OSINT) system that collects and analyzes publicly available material. According to the reports, some information that is not classified was exposed. Classified material and classified systems were reportedly not breached.
When the two agencies discovered the breach has not been disclosed. What information was exposed and who the attacker is have not been revealed either.

timeline.event: The New York Times reported that the CIA and ODNI had recently suffered a hack that exposed some unclassified information (local time).
AP reported, citing a source, that an unclassified CIA open-source intelligence system had been attacked and that the issue had been resolved.
An ODNI spokesperson told Reuters there had been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems. The CIA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Korean media, including Yonhap News, reported the incident citing foreign reports.

impact: Some unclassified information in the open-source intelligence analysis system was exposed (according to The New York Times).
Exactly what information was exposed has not been disclosed.
Classified material and classified systems were reportedly not breached (according to AP).
Information held by other federal agencies may also have been exposed, according to reports (according to The New York Times).
ODNI said there were no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems.
cause: According to reports, a hacker appears to have gained unauthorized access to at least one government system. The intrusion path and method have not been disclosed. The attacker's identity and who is behind the attack have not been confirmed.

The system analyzes material such as internet and social media content, commercial satellite imagery and data from private data brokers (according to AP and Yonhap News). Most of this material is public, but combining several data sets can be used to work out sensitive information, according to reports. The exact cause has not yet been determined.
response: The source cited by AP said the issue had been resolved. ODNI stated that there were no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems. The CIA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. What specific measures the two agencies took has not been disclosed.

The incident came to light amid a series of security incidents at US federal agencies. In the previous week, signs of an intrusion into the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database were reported. However, no evidence has been made public that the two incidents are related.

overview: Korea Investment Savings Bank's mobile website received abnormal access from outside. Customers' personal information was taken in the process. The bank posted a leak notice and an apology on its website (according to the company's notice and Asia Economy).

The first leak happened between the night of November 22 and the early hours of November 23 and affected 86,433 customers. On the morning of November 25, after the bank had blocked the access, the data of 178 more customers was leaked. In total, 86,611 customers are affected (according to The Financial News and Digital Daily).

The press described it as the largest personal data leak confirmed in the savings bank sector. Seven savings banks, including this one, have had confirmed breaches since September. No link between these incidents has been confirmed (according to Daily Secu).

timeline.event: From 10:42 p.m., abnormal outside access to the mobile website began (according to the company's notice and Asia Economy).
The access continued until 3:35 a.m., and the data of 86,433 customers was leaked. The bank found it the same day during a system check and blocked the access path.
The bank posted a personal data leak notice and an apology on its website (according to Daily Secu).
Between 9:43 and 10:02 a.m., the data of 178 more customers was leaked (according to Daily Secu and Digital Daily).
The Financial News, Asia Economy and other outlets reported the incident.

impact: The first leak exposed the data of 86,433 customers (according to the company's notice).
The additional leak on November 25 added 178 customers, for a total of 86,611 (according to The Financial News).
The leaked items are name, date of birth, gender, mobile phone number and connecting information (CI), five items in all.
The bank said financial transaction data such as account passwords was not leaked.
It is about twice the size of the previous largest savings bank leak, at Yegaram Savings Bank (43,246 people) (according to The Financial News).
The bank warned of follow-on harm such as voice phishing and spam text messages.
cause: The bank said the cause was abnormal outside access to its mobile website. The attacker and the exact intrusion method have not been disclosed (according to the company's notice).
A second leak happened after the blocking measures. It has not been confirmed whether the original weakness remained open or another route was used (according to Daily Secu).
response: The bank blocked the IP addresses and the abnormal access path used in the attack. It suspended the related services and applied new security policies. It said it has also strengthened system monitoring (according to Asia Economy and Digital Daily).

The bank opened a damage reporting center and a dedicated email address. It said it will verify claims and then proceed with relief. It advised customers to use the exposed personal information alert system and identity theft prevention services (according to Digital Daily).
CEO Jeon Chan-woo apologized and said the bank takes the matter very seriously. He said the bank will strengthen internal controls to prevent a repeat (according to The Financial News).
